questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Since I am studying Japanese Studies I have seen it as crucial to my studies to be able to go to Japan and immerse myself in the language and culture there.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Being able to go abroad has been a wonderful experience. However, I do find that the shift in academic level between Denmark and Japan a bit odd. I have taken seen that as mostly a part of a cultural exchange. What have been frustrating is overall the bureaucratic aspect of this exchange. The needed credits or ECTS has not lines up completely, and there has been very little understanding from either university. I would have loved to have had that as a pre-note before I went on exchange, that my chosen faculty did not offer up as many credits as KU wanted me to take.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: That was quite easy. Waseda sent out a thorough welcome package as well as an orientation meeting.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: - see above -

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Tokyo is a jungle for foreigners (Japan in general) to find housing in. Especially short term. I found and used a renting service called Fontana - that has furnished apartments in Tokyo. They were really sweet! The minimum stay is 3 months I think, but I would recommend them warmly to anyone going to Tokyo. You can also pay rent through Paypal or in person which means you do not need to set up a bank account, which saved me a great deal of trouble when I was only there for a little over 5 months. They were also super helpful whenever I wrote them, something in the apartment needed fixing, or when I needed to close my utility bills before leaving.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It's more expensive than campus, that's for sure. But! I got my own apartment for not that much more than a dorm would have been in Tokyo. You have to pay utilities on your own, and the trash system in Japan is tricky but! My landlord was super sweet about helping and guiding me so I can only warmly recommend them.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
The information about housing and the application for it was super late. I got an email a month before coming to Tokyo that I wouldn't be getting a Waseda Dorm... But that they could set me up with an off campus partner (even that wasn't sure). In fear of being homeless in Tokyo, I started searching for my own apartment. I was lucky enough that they actually did give me the possibility of an off campus partner dorm, but I would not have had my own bathroom - and for about 1500kr more each month I got my own apartment. 
Of course the information about this off-campus partner dorm came around 3 weeks before my arrival.. And one of the other exchange students from KU did not get one and also had to go look for her own accommodation. So I am happy that I had already found an apartment through Fontana.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Most of it was through an online form, no need for an TOEFL test - which is nice. I think it was fairly easy as far as I remember.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Their webpage is a bit of a jungle, but I stuck with one faculty (SILS) and read about that one. They are quite sweet to answer emails if needed.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: The registration for course system at Waseda is a complete lottery. Which is super stressful, and continues into semester start. There are three rounds of lottery, and you are not guaranteed any courses. I would NOT recommend it to anyone who has to have a very specific course - because they can't help you. If you get in you get in, and they don't take any requirements from home universities into consideration.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Do not fall in love with any specific courses, but have at least 10 different you can see yourself apply to. Don't stress necessarily beforehand - you can't do anything about it anyway. If you don't get in within the first three rounds of application, they have what they call "relief course registration". Then you will get placed at a course where they have space left - which is either A) less popular courses or B) courses somebody has dropped since they got something else in the second or third registration round.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It reminded me of highschool. Attendance, much homework, lectures where no involvement was needed, tests all the time. The academic level was low, and nobody expected much of you. But you still had to be there, to hand in homework. In my experience it was quantity over quality.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: It wasn't any problem. Nothing too complicated of what I took. When on exchange at SILS you are not allowed to take introiuctinary courses, so be aware of that.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Lecture based, no discussions in barely any classes I took. Each class is a 100 minutes without break.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Anthropology of Religion, Japanese Art History, Jazz History, Comprehensive Japanese 4, Picture books in Japanese 3-5.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The Jazz course was the best course that I had. But, I fear it was the last time it was provided as the teacher went on to be retired. The Anthropology of Religion has interesting reading and ethnographic films but the workload (even if the quality of it doesn't matter) became a bit troublesome. The picture books in Japanese was fun! We read picture books together and discussed them in Japanese. Then we had to write weekly reviews in Japanese, and in the end make a picture book each that we had to present! It was a great way of expanding vocabulary.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Buying stuff for my apartment. It was furnished but I still needed personal items as well as cleaning supplies and cloths racks.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: The national health insurance was way less expensive than I had thought!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: If you want to, you can join a club at the university. There are ALL kind of clubs. They take up a lot of time though. There were also a good bit of introduction parties and such when the semester started.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend trying to attend some sort of festival! There are plenty, for all seasons, in Japan. It's great fun!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Travel, travel, travel. Even if it's just day trips from Tokyo, do it! The public transport system in Japan is easy to follow and can take you far and near. I would really recommend looking around not only the inner city but also outside of it.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy. I have also traveled many times to Japan, and studies Japanese for quite a while.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Not really.. The faculty I studied at had international students, and Japanese students with an international focus. I must admit I ended up with being friends with mostly international students.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The academic culture was probably my biggest challenge.. I am used to analysing and trying to form my own meaning about everything. It was quite a challenge to just take in lectures and then do no discussion.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The food!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Don't take more than the minimum amount of credits. It's busy enough as it is. Make use of the library and group rooms/study rooms - Waseda has really good facilities.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Have fun OUTSIDE of the university. You will have many classes on the BA level, and so much homework.. But remember: the level is not as all as high as on KU. Quantity over quality!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting other exchange students, and being able to live in Japan!

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Finding meaning in doing school on this level again.. It put a lid on the academic passion I admit. Also that everybody used chatGPT.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
